Although the study of disease transmission on urban transit has frequently employed well-mixed models, these approaches often overlook the spatially structured nature of the urban environment. This paper argues that integrating well-mixed frameworks with spatially explicit representations of urban mobility offers significant advantages for forecasting disease spread among urban transit users. We illustrate this through the case of SARS-CoV-2 transmission on a specific urban bus route, utilizing a well-mixed model enhanced with spatially structured mobility data. The results indicate that this hybrid approach yields more accurate transmission rate estimates and refined basic reproduction number ($R_0$) calculations compared to traditional well-mixed models. Consequently, we recommend incorporating spatially structured mobility data into well-mixed epidemiological frameworks to enhance the precision of disease transmission predictions.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect (SOPE) enables the induction of significant spin-orbit coupling in materials lacking intrinsic SO interactions through contact with adjacent high-SO materials, a phenomenon critical for advancing spintronic technologies. This study employs first-principles calculations to investigate the interfacial SOPE within Co/Bi multilayers, specifically examining how interface characteristics influence the effect. Our findings reveal that the SOPE in Co/Bi systems is governed by the hybridization between Co and Bi orbitals at the interface. Specifically, a chemically bonded interface facilitates stronger spin-orbit coupling compared to a more isolated interface. Additionally, we demonstrate that both the direction and magnitude of the induced spin-orbit coupling are dictated by the specific interfacial atomic configuration. Finally, we applied this framework to analyze the interfacial geometry of the Co/Bi heterostructure exhibiting giant SO-to-charge conversion, offering a rational explanation for its observed performance.

This paper investigates the time-independent fractional Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for the generalized Mie-type potential using the Jumarie fractional derivative. By applying an appropriate ansatz for the wavefunction, the equation is reduced to a fractional differential form. Analytical solutions are derived for various potentials within this framework, with particular emphasis on the generalized Mie-type potential. The corresponding radial fractional wavefunctions and fractional expectation values of the radius and momentum are computed for the generalized Mie-type potential. Finally, the results are illustrated graphically to visually demonstrate their characteristics.

This study examines the application of gradient-based optimization methods for deriving effective Lipschitz constants for neural networks, with the goal of imposing these constraints during training. We introduce a novel, data-dependent Lipschitz measure that functions as a regularization term within the standard neural network loss. Our approach employs a convex relaxation of the non-convex optimization problem required to determine the exact Lipschitz value, utilizing a novel, computationally efficient metric that relies on singular value decompositions of Jacobian matrices. We evaluate our method on both synthetic and real-world datasets, including ImageNet, to assess its impact on classification performance under various attack scenarios.

This study examines the NLO QCD corrections to the $l^+l^-$ production process at high invariant mass within third-generation gauge vector leptoquark models. We implement this using QCD@NLO and MadGraph5_aMC@NLO, integrating the NLO PS scheme via the POWHEG-BOX framework. We analyze the perturbative stability of the NLO results and compare them against LO predictions. Furthermore, we assess the impact of varying parton distribution functions and unregulated scales on the NLO cross section. Finally, we explore the necessity of NLO corrections by comparing our findings with LHC data.

Using uncertainty-aware multimodal deep learning, we have developed a dose-reduction framework for positron emission tomography (PET) that enhances low-dose images with details from higher-dose sources. Although existing uncertainty-guided multimodal methods effectively integrate high-quality information into noisy inputs, they often fail when encountering out-of-distribution (OOD) high-dose images, potentially introducing high-frequency artifacts. To address this, we introduce a novel approach, PU-M3S, which employs three key innovations: (1) a convolutional autoencoder to generate high-dose OOD images from low-dose inputs, (2) a Bayesian convolutional neural network to estimate uncertainty for both OOD and non-OOD high-dose images, and (3) a learning strategy prioritizing pixels with low uncertainty during pixel-wise regression. Experiments on real cardiac data demonstrate that PU-M3S produces superior results compared to current methods, effectively restoring high-dose image features into low-dose OOD datasets.

Centering Theory (Grosz et al., 1995; Regier & Goldberg, 1996) offers a robust framework for understanding how coreference functions within natural language discourse. This study investigates the theory's applicability to neural coreference resolution models, which typically operate on single-paragraph texts. We trained a neural coreference resolver using Wikipedia's abstracts, while also developing a dedicated algorithm to identify long-distance coreferences within these short passages. Our findings reveal that Centering Theory is less effective at capturing coreference within brief texts compared to its performance on extended discourses. Furthermore, we observed that the theory struggles with coreference phenomena involving anaphora, cataphora, and coreference among non-pronominal entities. These insights carry significant implications for designing and deploying neural coreference resolution systems.

WiFi signal strength is frequently utilized to approximate the distance between a device and an access point. This approach typically involves supervised machine learning, which requires an initial site survey to collect training data—a process that is often labor-intensive and costly. This paper introduces a streamlined method for generating such training datasets using a mobile application designed for both iOS and Android platforms. The app enables users to input coordinates via GPS while automatically capturing the Received Signal Strength (RSS) values for all visible access points. We evaluated this technique in three distinct environments: a university campus, a hospital, and a shopping mall. The resulting machine learning models were tested using data from unseen locations and devices to assess their generalization capabilities. Furthermore, we developed and compared multiple estimation algorithms, identifying a simple linear regression model as the optimal choice based on the lowest root mean square error (RMSE). The final system achieved an average RMSE of 2.3 meters, with results varying between 1.8 and 3.1 meters depending on the specific setting.

Beam breakup instability poses a significant challenge for high-intensity electron accelerators, where feedback systems and operational strategies are often required to mitigate its effects. This paper examines how feedback performance and stability are influenced by filling patterns in energy recovery linear accelerators (ERLs). We demonstrate that the choice of filling design introduces a previously unrecognized source of instability. Specifically, we analyze the Cornell ERL, showing that both the filling factor and the specific filling scheme alter the feedback system's open-loop gain and introduce new poles into the closed-loop transfer function. These findings indicate that optimizing filling designs is essential for maximizing feedback performance and overall beam stability.

We present the one-loop central-emission vertex for a single gluon radiated from a quark line within $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory, where the radiation originates from an adjacent gluon line. This calculation is performed in the foundational framework of the parton shower, utilizing the BFKL ladder formalism. The derived result is expressed as a Mellin-Barns integral, and we provide a numerical evaluation of its coefficients.

This study investigates the structural characteristics of end exclusion in molten polymer brushes, focusing on how the termination of tethered chains influences their conformation. By integrating a scaling framework with Monte Carlo simulations, we demonstrate that end exclusion is a universal phenomenon occurring across various surface geometries. Specifically, we analyze cylindrical brushes, where tethered ends segregate into a distinct layer near the interface, separating from the bulk of the chain. We further examine how stretching, tethering density, and surface curvature impact this organization. Additionally, we explore end distributions in conical and spherical brushes, revealing that the mechanism of end exclusion adapts to different surface curvatures. These findings offer essential insights into the structural principles governing end segregation in strongly stretched polymer systems.

The metric dimension of a connected graph $G$ represents the smallest possible cardinality of a resolving set for $G$. A subset $R$ qualifies as resolving if, for any distinct pair of vertices $u$ and $v$ in $G$, there exists at least one vertex $r$ in $R$ such that the distance from $u$ to $r$ differs from the distance from $v$ to $r$. This paper introduces the concept of trimmed metric dimension, defined as the minimum cardinality of a subset $R$ that satisfies the resolving condition and additionally ensures that no vertex in $R$ is equidistant to some pair of vertices in $G$. We investigate the properties of this dimension for several graph classes, including paths, cycles, complete graphs, complete bipartite graphs, stars, wheels, hypercubes, and various graphs with transitive or edge-transitive structures. Furthermore, we establish a general condition applicable to graphs possessing a specific type of symmetry that guarantees the trimmed metric dimension is strictly less than the standard metric dimension.

The paper outlines a machine learning approach applied to Fermi-LAT data, aiming to enhance the all-sky map by emphasizing variable sources. While the existing all-sky map serves as a primary tool for identifying gamma-ray sources, it often underemphasizes variability because it relies on photon counts, which are heavily weighted toward steady, bright sources. This study introduces a methodology using a linear model to generate an updated all-sky map that highlights source variability. The new map is compared against the current version, demonstrating that it effectively emphasizes variable sources, whereas the original map, driven by intensity, highlights the most luminous sources.

This paper introduces the serial monarchy, a novel framework for online optimization that merges the competitive and population-based approaches. In this model, an algorithm maintains a distribution of distributions over the decision space, selecting an action according to the current distribution while updating via a rule based on past performance. We establish a general update rule yielding polynomial sublinear polylogarithmic approximations to the population's regret across any problem with a bounded negative feedback range. Additionally, we analyze the method under negative feedback, demonstrating that the feedback received by selected options reflects the choices made by unselected ones. These insights allow us to adapt the general algorithm to specific domains, creating specialized solvers for online convex optimization with negative feedback, both unconstrained and constrained, as well as online combinatorial semi-bandit problems with similar feedback characteristics.

By leveraging this extensive dataset, we developed and implemented a novel detection algorithm specifically designed to identify binary asteroids. The method was tested on a sample of 1,000 known single asteroids, yielding a false positive rate of 0.0003 and a false negative rate of 0.0001. This paper introduces methods for estimating and testing hypotheses within network regression models that incorporate nonlinear components. These proposed techniques are applicable to a broad spectrum of network formation structures, covering both exogenous and various types of endogenous networks. The approach is designed to be versatile, allowing for the estimation of nonlinear functions derived from multiple, unconnected, or interconnected nodes. We establish the asymptotic properties of the proposed estimators and validate their performance through simulation experiments. The research concludes with an empirical analysis investigating how social media usage spreads among adolescents.

This paper introduces and analyzes a novel Leibniz rule tailored for Riemann-Liouvariable-order fractional integral and derivative operators. The core of this new formulation lies in the integrand of the expression, which encapsulates a variable-order fractional integral of the second kind involving one of the function components within the integral or derivative being processed. Crucially, this secondary function is selected to ensure the resulting expression adheres to the necessary regularity conditions. The authors establish several foundational properties of this specific class of operators and apply them to derive the complete Leibniz theorem. As a significant outcome of this research, the formula is successfully generalized to accommodate Riemann conditions.

We introduce IntentDnD, a framework designed to teach theory-of-mind (ToM) and intent recognition within human-agent interactions. In this setup, an agent converses with a human playing Dungeons and Dragons, utilizing ToM to infer the agent's mental states and intentions. We define a new task called IntentDnD, where the agent must infer the human's intentions from their utterances to generate more natural and engaging dialogue. We propose a novel method for human intent inference and a corresponding learning algorithm. Our results indicate that the agent significantly outperforms strong baselines in human preference evaluations regarding conversational quality and engagement. We also observe that the agent effectively learns intent recognition through these interactions. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/abhi1998/IntentDnD.

Proteins that form complex topologies exhibit unusual mechanical and functional traits, suggesting that knot formation is a regulated process. In this study, we investigate the mechanical unfolding pathways of knotted proteins by analyzing the trajectories of chain bending. We introduce a quantitative measure for the topological complexity of a knot relative to an unknotted state and utilize this metric to identify the most probable bending pathways. Our analysis reveals that, compared to their topologically equivalent unknotted counterparts, proteins containing knots uncoil along distinct routes characterized by higher curvature and torsion. Furthermore, we observe that the specific geometry of the knot significantly influences the unfolding mechanism. These findings indicate that native-state knots impose structural constraints on the polypeptide backbone, thereby directing the selection of bending pathways during mechanical disintegration.

We determine the symplectic mapping category groups for specific sphere-blowup tori, utilizing these findings alongside previously established results for projective spaces and the 4-torus to derive the symplectic mapping category groups for all positive integer $n$-dimensional real projective spaces $\mathbb{R}P^n$ and $k$-fold iterated torus blowups.

This monograph offers a comprehensive overview of the Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem, detailing its derivation and the classification of NG modes. It examines the application of the NG theorem across diverse systems, including relativistic and nonrelativistic theories, as well as those with and without gauge invariance. Special attention is given to the classification of NG modes and the formulation of their effective Lagrangians. The work also explores the theorem's relevance in various physical contexts, such as high-energy physics, condensed matter systems, and string theory.

We introduce D3DD, a novel framework designed to enhance the instruction-following capabilities of generic chatbots by leveraging large language models (LLMs) to generate synthetic, high-quality labeled data. Unlike current approaches that rely on creating numerous diverse real-world hypothetical scenarios, our method demonstrates that a smaller set of diverse *phrasal* hypotheticals is equally effective for training. We utilize a cost-effective LLM to produce a compact dataset of diverse real-world hypothetical examples, which we then employ to fine-tune base chat models. Our experiments indicate that these trained models achieve performance on par with those trained using vast amounts of complex hypothetical data.

Thin films of full Heusler alloys, such as Cu$_2$MnSn (CMS), are frequently deposited on substrates like Si or sapphire to induce strain and modify their electronic properties. In these configurations, film growth typically proceeds via van der Waals (vdW) epitaxy, which facilitates the formation of nanoscale domains and defects. However, growing such domains on conductive superlattices or graphene remains a significant challenge. This study demonstrates that depositing Cu$_2$MnSn on graphene placed atop a sapphire substrate results in a polycrystalline structure composed of small grains (approximately 20 nm) separated by distinct grain boundaries. Transmission electron microscopy reveals that these domains are pinned by dislocations and exhibit a 90-degree rotation relative to the underlying graphene lattice. Furthermore, the study highlights that the equilibrium between vdW epitaxy and pinhole epitaxy can be regulated by adjusting the deposition temperature.

In many classification scenarios, acquiring training data that accurately represents the problem is difficult. To address this, we introduce a method for generating multi-label samples from single positive labels. Our approach first employs a standard classifier trained on single positive labels to create an initial pool of multi-label examples. Subsequently, we apply a multi-label classifier to refine this initial pool. We evaluate our method on three real-world datasets: Amazon, DBLP, and TREC. Our evaluation shows that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques for multi-label sample generation across all three datasets.

We establish a 2-categorical equivalence between the 2-category of observables, states, and quantum systems and the 2-category of complex Hilbert spaces, linear maps, and their structures. This result offers a fresh, rigorous perspective on the foundational framework for quantum mechanics originally proposed by Jacobson and Clifton.

We investigate the potential for nearby radio galaxies to produce detectable high-energy gamma-rays, focusing on the electromagnetic output of accretion disks surrounding their central supermassive black holes. While such disks often experience outflows and exhibit X-ray emissions, the associated high-energy gamma-rays typically remain undetected. To address this, we employ numerical simulations of disk dynamics to explore the role of magnetic fields in driving these systems. Our findings indicate that disks characterized by strong magnetism and low effective temperatures become spatially confined by magnetic pressure, forming "magnetically restricted disks." We demonstrate that these confined disks can generate gamma-rays through inverse Compton scattering, potentially explaining the missing high-energy emissions observed in various X-ray binaries and radio galaxies.

Heart sound classification is a vital non-invasive technique for diagnosing cardiac disorders. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to categorize heart sounds into normal and pathological groups, utilizing raw cardiac signals processed through two distinct artificial neural networks: a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) adapted for one-dimensional data and a Residual Neural Network (ResNet). To enhance the efficacy of the 1D-CNN, raw signals were transformed using two methods: a novel approach termed "convolutional distortion" and a traditional "additive noise" technique. The model was evaluated on a private dataset comprising 1,000 recordings of normal hearts and 1,000 recordings of diseased hearts. Evaluation results indicate that the proposed 1D-CNN architecture, specifically when trained on signals distorted via convolutional distortion, achieved a 99.99% accuracy rate.

Wearable health devices are increasingly prevalent, yet their ability to accurately diagnose and monitor diseases is hindered by the need for extensive labeled datasets. Traditional methods relying on centralized data aggregation struggle with privacy concerns and are often ineffective in wearable healthcare due to domain shifts between different data sources. To address these challenges, we introduce FedHealth, a federated transfer knowledge framework designed to improve model performance on target tasks using only locally collected data. FedHealth integrates federated learning with transfer learning to enhance the accuracy of health-related classification tasks. Specifically, we utilize the statistical properties of source task data as knowledge to guide the target task, thereby reducing dependency on large volumes of labeled data. Furthermore, we employ a dynamic knowledge update mechanism to continuously refine the source model by incorporating newly acquired labeled data. Comprehensive experiments conducted on three real-world datasets demonstrate that FedHealth significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches.

This paper examines various higher-moment portfolio optimization techniques, analyzing their mathematical structures to reveal underlying connections. We introduce a unified framework that organizes these approaches, demonstrating how they can be expressed as quadratic programming problems. Additionally, we propose a novel class of efficient frontiers specifically designed for tailoring investment strategies based on investor preferences regarding skewness and kurtosis.

This study introduces a novel method for enhancing the efficiency of software systems by applying automatic post-processing to their outputs. This approach is specifically designed to handle scenarios where existing system limitations prevent developers from executing immediate updates or patches. By systematically analyzing raw data generated after deployment, the proposed technique identifies and addresses inherent flaws, thereby elevating overall system performance and reliability without requiring direct modifications to the original codebase.

This paper introduces an optimal switching control framework where both entry and exit cost functions are potentially discontinuous, thereby requiring treatment as cost processes with regulated paths. We establish the existence of an optimal control and demonstrate, through a novel application of a stochastic compactness argument to the control processes themselves, the convergence of an associated penalized problem. Furthermore, if the cost functions satisfy specific monotonicity conditions, the unique optimality of the control process is proven. Finally, we address the numerical approximation of this control process via a discrete-time scheme.

We present a new model for interstellar carbon monoxide (CO) that incorporates non-thermal heating mechanisms alongside radiative transfer calculations. This approach is essential for explaining the unexpectedly high brightness temperatures observed in the low-excitation C i lines within molecular gas reservoirs, where radiative equilibrium alone fails to account for such emission. Our findings indicate that Low-J CO lines in these regions are subthermally excited, a phenomenon driven by the elevated kinetic temperatures resulting from non-thermal processes. Consequently, the standard method of estimating kinetic temperature via the critical density of CO transitions becomes invalid. Instead, we demonstrate that the kinetic temperature can be accurately derived from the ratio of Low-J to high-J CO line intensities, utilizing the same non-thermal heating framework required to explain the previously noted over-thermalization of Low-excitation C i transitions.

This paper examines the sequence reconstruction problem defined by the Hamming distance specifically for permutations. We introduce a novel algorithm that successfully solves this problem using exactly $n(n-1)/2$ matrices, where $n$ represents the length of the row strings within those matrices. Additionally, we establish a lower bound indicating that a minimum of $\Omega(n^2/\log n)$ matrices are required to solve the problem when strings are drawn from a random distribution.

Pulsar Timing Arrays are poised to detect gravitational waves from supermassive black hole binaries in the near future. This study investigates the computational efficiency of calculating post-Newtonian corrections for eccentric inspiriting binaries within a Gaussian process-based inference framework used by PTOA collaborations. We introduce a novel algorithm to determine these higher-order terms and benchmark it against existing methods. Our findings indicate that incorporating post-Newtonian precision for eccentric binaries via Gaussian process modeling is feasible, with a modest increase in processing time that diminishes as binary eccentricity approaches zero.

The ALEXIS process represents the most elementary model of an interacting particle system evolving on $\mathbb{Z}^2$, featuring independent asymmetric simple random walks along horizontal lines and dependent, symmetric random walks with a specific hopping rate on vertical lines. This article examines the process when initialized with a step configuration, demonstrating that the resulting vertical trajectories constitute the velocity process for asymmetric simple random walks along a single line. Furthermore, it establishes that the model's multi-particle dynamics can be equivalently described as a queueing system with infinite capacity, where service rates vary according to queue length.

Mathematical epidemiological models have long served as a vital tool for investigating infectious disease outbreaks. This article offers a review of the principal models developed for the current SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, detailing the mathematical formulation of key epidemiological parameters such as transmission and recovery rates. Furthermore, it explores the application of these models to real-world data from the novel coronavirus epidemic. The discussion encompasses both classical frameworks and recent innovations, including Bayesian approaches and machine learning techniques. Finally, the text addresses the inherent challenges associated with these models and the interpretation of their outcomes.

Atom-molecule conversion represents a fundamental many-body quantum phenomenon, yet achieving it with spinor atoms has remained elusive due to the typically weak intermolecular interactions. We demonstrate that laser-driven three-body recombination can facilitate spinor atom-molecule transformation by engineering strong artificial intermolecular couplings. Within a two-component system, we establish a mapping where the two molecular states correspond to the three spinor atom states, thereby creating an effective two-level quantum model. This approach enables the generation of various spinor regimes—including antiferromagnetic, ferromagnetic, and resonant configurations—by precisely adjusting the laser parameters. Specifically, we construct a spinor antiferromagnetic model characterized by an induced long-range interaction. Furthermore, we detail the dynamics of atom-molecule conversion within these induced many-body frameworks.

DNA storage offers a massive capacity for digital information, yet current protocols struggle with limited support for data structures and update mechanisms. This paper introduces a new coding scheme that effectively combines the Long Short Code (LSC) and DNA Hash Code (DHC) methods to construct a hierarchical, update-capable system. By integrating LSC's ability to represent tree structures with DHC's efficient data encoding, our approach enables storage of complex hierarchies using short, synthetic DNA strands. We demonstrate that this new code maintains high storage efficiency and low error rates, while also supporting data modifications and hierarchical navigation through hybridization-based operations. Furthermore, we present a novel strategy to resolve hash collisions during retrieval. Experimental results indicate that our scheme achieves near-optimal efficiency and successfully facilitates search and update tasks within hierarchical data.

We introduce a novel deep learning framework designed to solve the shallow water equations (SWEs), a set of nonlinear partial differential equations critical for modeling large-scale fluid dynamics. By employing a convolutional neural network (CNN) to approximate the solution $u(x,t)$, our method offers a computationally efficient alternative to traditional numerical solvers. We validate our approach against established benchmarks, demonstrating that the learned solutions align closely with exact and numerical data. Furthermore, we apply the model to simulate dam-break scenarios, highlighting its potential for real-time applications in fluid dynamics.

High-dynamic-range (HDR) imaging is achieved by merging multiple exposures of a scene to cover an extended dynamic range. This paper introduces a system that automatically and acquires these exposures on a smartphone, utilizing automatic exposure settings while dynamically adjusting them based on real-time feedback. The system leverages a novel, efficient feedback mechanism to determine the optimal automatic exposure range and count, ensuring the resulting images are merged without tone mapping. Experiments demonstrate that this approach outperforms current methods in terms of HDR range, acquisition speed, and user-friendliness.

Causal deep learning aims to integrate deep neural networks with causal graphical models to enhance capabilities in non-stationary environments, support decision-making, support counterfactual reasoning, and ensure robustness. However, the sheer volume of potential causal deep structures within a complex setting often hinders the identification of the most suitable architecture. We propose that navigation through this vast design space can be facilitated by a purpose-built library of deep network modules, each tailored to specific estimators for particular causal structures. We introduce CausalVoxels, a semantic-semantic 3D semantic space designed to organize these modules. By positioning deep structures within CausalVoxels, we can leverage 3D visualization to facilitate the selection of appropriate designs. We evaluate our framework using three diverse datasets covering both supervised and unsupervised scenarios: policy evaluation, image generation, and image classification.

This paper presents a new proof of the Mumford conjecture, which asserts that the universal closed oriented surface of dimension two, denoted as $\mathcal{M}_{g}^{1}$, has the same stable homology as a coefficient ring extension of the relative homology of the mapping class group, $\text{MCG}(S_{g})$. The argument relies on the $b$-principle, specifically demonstrating that the $b$-principle is not applicable to the mapping class group, thereby establishing the result through a negative application of this principle.

Cardiac mechanics simulations are frequently employed to investigate cardiac pathologies and evaluate therapeutic strategies. However, these simulations face significant computational hurdles due to the nonlinear nature of hyperelastic material models and the extensive spatial and temporal extents of the cardiac domain. To address these challenges, this study offers a comparative evaluation of two multilevel preconditioning techniques—specifically Full Multigrid (FMG) and Geometric Multigrid (GMG)—applied within a finite element framework utilizing an augmented Lagrangian approach for the linearized equations of motion. Our analysis indicates that while both methods exhibit comparable efficiency, FMG generates a more consistent reduction in residual error across iterations. Furthermore, we detail the implementation of a novel, efficient boundary correction mechanism within the GMG algorithm to enhance its performance.

Standard Brownian motion, characterized by a Gaussian distribution of particle displacements and linear growth of the mean squared displacement (MSD) with time, serves as the baseline for comparing diffusion processes. This study investigates the connection between the time-evolution of the MSD and the random nature of the diffusion coefficient. Specifically, we examine how various scenarios of random diffusivity—spanning independent and dependent processes, stationary and non-stationary conditions, and both Markovian and non-Markovian frameworks—result in anomalous diffusion that deviates from Gaussian behavior. We further analyze the impact of different spatial correlations on these processes. The work is framed within the generalized diffusion equation, utilizing the time-fractional operator to model the temporal dynamics of the mean squared displacement.

This study introduces a generalized theoretical framework for analyzing the linear and nonlinear coupling between optical resonator modes, waveguide modes, and both guided and leaky modes. This approach offers a unified description of diverse physical phenomena, including the formation of bound states in the continuum, exceptional points, and the generation of solitons and resonances. The theory derives the equations governing the amplitudes of these modes, which are determined by the overlap integrals between the fields of the interacting modes. We apply this framework to examine Kerr nonlinear interactions within a specific setup: a waveguide positioned near a leaky mode of an optical resonator. The results indicate that the coupled system can support both high-$Q$ and bound states in the continuum, with the conditions for these states depending on the alignment between the waveguide and the resonator.

Enhancing the temporal resolution of fluid flow data offers a promising avenue for investigating fluid dynamics, yet it remains a challenging task due to the high computational costs associated with traditional numerical simulations like Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS). This study introduces a flow-specific Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) designed to enhance the temporal resolution of turbulent flows at various Reynolds numbers. By training this model on DNS data of turbulent channel flow, we enhanced the temporal resolution of both velocity and Reynolds stress tensors by a factor of 16. Comparative analysis demonstrates that our proposed FSGAN significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of both velocity and stress field reconstruction. Furthermore, increasing the temporal resolution of these enhanced datasets reveals that, at higher sub-sampling rates, undersampling induces distinct non-stationary artifacts in the stresses. These findings indicate that high temporal fidelity is essential for accurately capturing the statistical properties of turbulent flows.

We introduce L2Explorer, a dynamic lifelong reinforcement learning (RL) evaluation benchmark featuring diverse, evolving subtasks. Unlike current RL benchmarks that rely on static tasks, L2Explorer enables continuous interaction across an infinite sequence of evolving tasks, with new objectives emerging from prior experiences. The environment incorporates dynamic elements such as shifting reward structures, novel state variables, and new action spaces, ensuring the need for agents to continuously adapt. We evaluated L2Explorer on prominent reinforcement learning algorithms, demonstrating its effectiveness in assessing and advancing lifelong learning capabilities.

Process mining has emerged as a vital field for analyzing and understanding business processes, yet existing methods often struggle with massive process logs, necessitating significant memory that hampers real-time analysis. This paper introduces a novel streaming-based exploration and monitoring methodology designed to handle process data in real time. The approach decomposes the task into three core components: filtering, aggregation, and visualization. By leveraging the StreamBase SQL language, the authors developed a prototype system to demonstrate these techniques. The proposed method was validated against a dataset of 1.5 billion events, successfully handling the data with only 1.5 gigabytes of RAM.

This work explores the relationship between algebraic and analytic forms of moduli spaces, specifically focusing on their extensions and mutual interactions. It presents a generalization of the Serre extension theorem applicable to families of curves within arbitrary moduli spaces. Additionally, it addresses the converse inquiry: under what conditions does an algebraic space qualify as analytic.

We utilize a high-resolution, 100 pc-resolution simulation of a Milky Way-like galaxy to investigate the mechanisms behind the decline of the galaxy main sequence at high stellar masses. Our analysis of the specific star formation rate (sfr) as a function of total mass ($M_{\star}$) reveals a downturn that aligns with observations, contrasting with the continuous rise predicted by subgrid star formation prescriptions based on gas surface density. Our findings indicate that this behavior originates from the shift from disk to bulge dominance in the $M_{\star}$ distribution at high values, which suppresses specific star formation rates due to lower gas fractions and elevated stellar mass surface densities in the bulge. Consequently, our results suggest that current star formation models, which fail to account for the distinct physical conditions within galactic nuclei, are a primary cause for the mismatch between the observed and predicted star formation rate–mass scaling.

This study introduces a cross-lingual sentiment analysis framework based on multilabel classification, designed to tackle the challenge of evaluating emotional tones in foreign languages using only monolingual training data. The proposed model integrates three core components: a dynamic bidirectional long short-term memory (D-BiLSTM) module for enhanced feature representation, a cross-task architecture to leverage shared linguistic patterns, and a cross-language mechanism grounded in multilabel classification to utilize unlabeled target domain data. Validated on three distinct datasets, the approach demonstrates superior performance compared to existing methods, achieving a 0.5\% increase in F1 score on the English (Ennli) dataset, a 0.6\% improvement on the German (SemEval-2014 Task 1) dataset, and a 0.7\% gain on the Chinese (SoC 2014) dataset relative to the best baseline.

Rapidly and accurately identifying severe cases of COVID-19 is critical for effective resource allocation and patient care. We propose a novel method that analyzes chest X-rays to detect the need for Intensive Care Unit (ICU) admission in infected individuals. Our dataset comprises 1,500 images from infected individuals, categorized into four classes based on infection severity: Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Non-infection. We introduce a new convolutional neural network architecture designed to classify these severity levels and specifically identify the "Severe" category. This approach relies on a multi-task learning framework utilizing an attention-based mechanism to classify severity and isolate the "Severe" class, while simultaneously extracting features from Non-infected, Mild, and Moderate cases to distinguish them from one another. Our dataset includes 1,500 images, with 375 contributed by each of the four classes. We evaluated our model using five-fold cross-validation, achieving an F1 score of 0.87 for detecting severe infections. The proposed method demonstrates high efficacy in identifying severe COVID-19 cases from X-ray data, with particular relevance to distinguishing these patients for necessary ICU care.
This paper demonstrates that the universal simplicial collection functions as a simplicial group.

Visual relationship detection (VRD) aims to identify and classify the connections between interacting objects within an image. A pressing challenge in this domain is handling "erroneous positives," where the system produces false detections of object pairs that do not genuinely exist. This paper investigates the root causes behind such incorrect positives and proposes a novel framework designed to eliminate them. Our approach leverages a new dataset of negative instance images, termed NVD, which captures non-exemplar object pairs. By integrating NVD with a standard exemplar-based detector, we train the system to distinguish between real and false positive relationships. Experiments on the standard VRD dataset demonstrate that our method significantly boosts recall for object pairs while simultaneously reducing erroneous detections.

We analyze the ~3 gigahertz (GHz) galaxy cluster containing NGC 4993, which recently hosted a type Ia supernova, using multi-wavelength data to investigate its history. Our study reveals that NGC 4993 is a massive (~10^11 solar masses) system exhibiting a central bulge, an outer asymmetric stellar disk, and a kinematic disturbance likely caused by a recent major merger ~3 gigahertz (GHz) ago. Despite these features, the galaxy maintains a low specific star formation rate and lacks significant cold gas or recent star formation. We argue that this configuration—a bulge embedded within a misaligned, intrinsically edge-on disk—indicates a structural transformation triggered by accretion. We further suggest the bulge formed via rapid, in-situ star formation fueled by gas inflows induced by the merger event. Finally, we compare NGC 4993 to similar galaxies to explore the role of mergers in the formation of early-type galaxies.

This study examines the November 7, 2004, solar flare (X1.0B), which generated a solar neutron decay (SND) signature in gamma-ray data collected by the RHESSI satellite. The analysis reveals that the electron acceleration responsible for this event occurred in two distinct phases: an initial impulsive phase and a subsequent, more prolonged phase. The findings indicate that the electron acceleration mechanism was triggered by magnetic reconnection events situated above the flare's soft X-ray emission loops. Furthermore, the research suggests that the magnetic field configuration within the active region evolved from a closed system to an open one, facilitating the escape of neutron decay photons into space.

The discovery of KIC 9832224, a rapidly rotating solar-type star hosting a transiting planet, presents a significant challenge to standard models of star-planet interactions. While theoretical frameworks predict that such a system should have experienced significant orbital decay due to tidal forces, the observed orbital period remains stable. Furthermore, current theories of angular momentum transport fail to account for the star's high rotation rate. To address these discrepancies, we conducted hydrodynamic simulations exploring various mechanisms of angular momentum transfer. Our results indicate that the ingestion of the planet provides the necessary angular momentum to explain the system's rapid rotation while maintaining orbital stability.

Rapidly spreading fake news across social media and news platforms poses significant threats to public safety and social stability. Traditional detection methods have primarily focused on textual data, often overlooking the rich contextual information available in multimedia formats. Furthermore, existing models struggle to effectively integrate textual and visual features, missing the synergistic potential of combining them. This paper introduces a novel meta neural process network designed for emergent false news detection that utilizes both text and images. This architecture addresses two key challenges: first, it employs a neural process to model the distribution of existing image-text based samples, enabling the generation of synthetic fake news datasets even from small initial sets; and second, it facilitates the transfer of knowledge from these generated samples to new, unseen multimodal fake news instances. Consequently, the proposed method can leverage insights from a limited multimodal fake news dataset to detect similar content elsewhere, despite the scarcity of large-scale labeled data. Extensive experiments on three standard benchmark datasets confirm the superiority of our approach compared to current state-of-the-art detection methods.

This study examines the 1D incompressible transport equation where the velocity field is derived from a $n$-th order circulation operator. We demonstrate that if this velocity field exhibits a jump discontinuity across a single point, any initial singularity present will be transported without alteration. Conversely, if the velocity field is continuous, any initial singularity will be smoothed out within a finite timeframe.

In the context of array signal processing, polyphase Golay complementary arrays (PGCAs) represent a class of structures characterized by two PGCAs of identical dimensions, where the combined array exhibits a gcoherence function that remains constant. This study introduces novel construction methods for PGCNs, specifically targeting prime array lengths $p$ with an even coherence value $k$. For these parameters, explicit designs are provided that achieve the theoretical upper bound on the number of phases, reaching $\min(p-1,p+1)$ for the specified $p$ and $k$. Additionally, for any arbitrary size $N$, a recursive algorithm is developed to synthesize PGCNs of that dimension with a phase count of $O(\log(N))$.

Silicon has recently attracted significant attention for its potential in quantum computing, largely due to the demonstration of two-qubit gates and the ability to swap qubit states between two silicon spin qubits. This work introduces a novel approach to spin swapping that relies on quantum interference occurring at atomic-scale junctions within silicon nanowires. By utilizing this method, researchers can achieve a fidelity of 99.9% for two-qubit operations, surpassing current limits set by existing gates. The work also establishes a new benchmark for silicon quantum computing by demonstrating that these interference-based gates remain effective despite variations in fabrication imperfections.

The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, particularly deep learning, has enabled the analysis of massive datasets across diverse fields. Among these developments, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a leading approach for processing structured data organized as graphs. This survey provides a comprehensive review of recent breakthroughs in GNNs, with a specific focus on their application to dynamic systems. We introduce a unified framework for analyzing complex systems by modeling their interactions as graphs, detailing how to learn from and predict the evolution of these dynamic structures. Additionally, we examine emerging trends in generative modeling of complex systems and discuss the significant challenges that lie ahead in this evolving area.

Accurately predicting individual brain trauma outcomes is critical for effective post-injury care, yet it remains difficult due to the scarcity of injury data and the complexity of the injury itself. This study introduces a novel Generative Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoder (GPAVAE) architecture designed to simulate diverse brain injuries. By leveraging this synthetic injury data, machine learning classifiers can be trained with greater robustness and accuracy. We evaluated the GPAVAE on a dataset of 1,000 CT scans, successfully generating realistic lesions that matched the anatomical patterns of the original images. Furthermore, we validated the clinical utility of these simulated injuries by training a neural network classifier, which demonstrated marked improvements in both accuracy and robustness when assessed on injured versus non-inected data.

GP 2 is a concurrent, general-purpose programming language designed to be compiled into efficient C code. This work presents the Enhanced GP 2 (E-GP 2) compiler, which improves upon the original GP 2 by generating more compact and optimized binaries. Key enhancements include the use of a graph-based register allocator, a sophisticated instruction scheduler, and a novel memory management strategy. Benchmark results demonstrate that E-GP 2 outperforms the standard GP 2 compiler in both execution speed and memory efficiency.

Feature extraction is a critical step in many machine learning workflows, yet designing effective extraction methods remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces a unified framework grounded in contrastive learning to address this issue. We propose a general structure for feature extraction via contrastive learning and establish a theoretical basis for its application. By integrating this framework into self-supervised learning, we achieve state-of-the-state performance on image classification benchmarks using only unlabeled data. Furthermore, when paired with supervised contrastive learning, the unified structure delivers state-of-the-state results on both image classification and natural language processing tasks, utilizing solely task-related unlabeled samples. These achievements highlight the framework's capacity to generate high-quality, generalizable features from unlabeled data, thereby reducing dependency on extensive labeled datasets.

This paper introduces an infinite family of graphs where, for each graph $\Gamma$ in the family, we establish that $\Gamma$ possesses the property of being star-normal. Specifically, $\Gamma$ is a quotient graph derived from a non-abelian, twisted wreath product of cyclic groups, with its automorphism group identified as $C(p^k) \rtimes C(p^k)$, where $p$ is a prime number and $k \geq 2$.

In the context of high-dimensional statistical modeling, categorical variables are typically encoded using one-hot representation, which transforms $J$ categories into $J$ binary features. We address the challenge of estimating regression coefficients for such variables by integrating group lasso regularization, ensuring that effects are learned jointly across categories within each variable. However, the inherent non-differentiability of the group lasso penalty function complicates optimization. To overcome this, we introduce a proximal gradient descent algorithm equipped with a novel proximal operator, enabling efficient minimization of the loss function. Additionally, we establish theoretical guarantees by proving non-asymptotic bounds for the proposed estimator. Finally, we validate the method's performance through extensive numerical simulations and real-world applications.

Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable generalization across various natural language processing tasks, their ability to handle domain-specific applications often relies on massive, unlabeled training data. This approach frequently incorporates noisy or irrelevant information, resulting in learned representations that lack explicit, actionable knowledge. Conversely, structured knowledge—such as medical guidelines, legal statutes, or encyclopedic entries—offers a distinct advantage by enabling precise control over model behavior. To bridge this gap, we introduce SKILL (Structured Knowledge Injection for Large Language Models), a framework designed to integrate such knowledge into an LLM's internal state. SKILL achieves this by systematically embedding knowledge into the model's hidden representations, ensuring that the resulting system retains the original capabilities while gaining access to injected information. We validate our method using T5 as a base, injecting both Wikipedia and PubMed data to create two new variants: SKILL-T5-Wiki and SKILL-T5-PubMed. Our experiments demonstrate that these versions significantly outperform standard T5 and other baselines across multiple natural language understanding benchmarks, with improvements ranging from 2.3 to 5.3 points. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that SKILL-Wiki enhances fact-based question answering, whereas SKILL-PubMed specifically boosts performance in medical natural language inference.

Line joins represent a critical yet frequently overlooked element in the anti-aliasing rendering of vector maps. This paper introduces a spatial anti-aliasing approach designed to enhance line joins, leveraging a 4-pixel $2\times2$ magnification technique. By integrating the algorithm with a rasterizer, it enables the seamless rendering of line joins within map applications. Furthermore, the method is adaptable to other map components, such as polygons and lines, ensuring broad utility in spatial visualization.

This paper introduces Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN), a novel model designed for multi-band single-channel audio enhancement. The architecture integrates a dual-path convolution recurrent network with a frequency-domain time convolutional network (FTCN). The FTCN component processes both high- and low-frequency bands separately, while the dual-path structure independently optimizes short- and long-term temporal dependencies. The model's efficacy was evaluated on the OpenMusicEnhancement (OME) dataset, where it secured the first position in the 2020 OpenMusicEnhancement Challenge. Additionally, quantitative results from the OME dataset and qualitative assessments from the OME demo platform confirm DPCRN's superior performance in audio enhancement.

This study introduces a new single-column model designed to simulate atmospheric convection involving multiple interacting fluids. The framework incorporates a thermodynamic model for binary mixtures and utilizes a set of coupled partial differential equations to represent the vertical profiles of temperature, composition, and velocity. These equations are solved using a semi-Lagrangian scheme for advection and an operator-splitting method for other terms. The model's performance is evaluated against a well-established spectral solver through simulations of a binary mixture subject to Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard instability. Results indicate that the new single-column approach effectively reproduces the thermal and compositional structures of convection rolls, as well as the probability density functions of temperature and concentration, even when the mixture exhibits phase separation under high Rayleigh numbers. This validation confirms the model's viability for future investigations into the complex dynamics of multi-fluid convection within the atmosphere.

We investigate the entanglement of two initially uncorrelated and separable two-level atoms interacting with independent single-mode electromagnetic fields via Jaynes-Cummings coupling. By analyzing the time-dependent entanglement of the composite system, we identify conditions under which entanglement reaches its theoretical maximum. Crucially, we demonstrate that even if the atoms begin in a completely separable state, non-zero coupling strengths can induce sincere entanglement. Specifically, when the atom-field coupling is sufficiently potent, the atoms become genuinely entangled regardless of the initial separability of the individual atom-field pairs.

This paper introduces a novel framework designed to evaluate the emotional tone of tweets regarding specific topics. The proposed method integrates an LSTM-based classifier with a dynamic, context-sensitive word embedding technique known as Doc2Vec. Evaluated on the semi-supervised Twitter Sentiment Analysis 2013 (TS2013) dataset, the model demonstrates strong performance, achieving a 0.8400 Area Under the Curve (AUC) value and a 0.7999 F1 score.

Entanglement tomography offers a method to reconstruct the entanglement of a quantum system using only local operations and classical communication, an approach that has been implemented via various techniques. This work introduces a novel entanglement manifestation within the tomogram, characterized by a transition from a continuous to a discrete structure. This phenomenon arises from the interplay between the inherent symmetry of the system's state and the non-commutativity of the measured observables. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the emergence of synchronization between subsystems also produces distinctive signatures within the tomogram. These findings are relevant for experimental efforts aimed at visualizing and analyzing quantum entanglement.

We introduce a method for inferring camera viewpoints in 360-degree tourism videos, addressing a significant hurdle in content analysis for immersive media. Our approach trains a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) to forecast camera orientation using subtitles, leveraging the fact that subtitles often reveal the current scene. To enhance subtitle reliability, we propose a filtering mechanism that removes low-quality subtitles, ensuring the model focuses on high-confidence textual cues. Furthermore, we introduce a novel textual representation that captures the spatial relationships between textual elements and visual content. Experiments conducted on a newly established 360-degree tourism dataset demonstrate the method's effectiveness in predicting both horizontal (yaw) and vertical (pitch) camera angles.

We introduce two novel locally precise tensor network algorithms designed to simulate the real-time dynamics and thermal equilibrium of lattice models. The first method, Variationally Precise Time-evolving Block-oligvector (VPE-TEBD), utilizes a parameterized unitary to construct the evolution operator, directly targeting the minimization of the Hamiltonian expectation value. The second approach, Locally Precise Purification (LPP), achieves a state of purified thermal equilibrium by minimizing the pure state energy within a locally precise framework. We demonstrate that both methods converge to highly accurate results with a system-wide inverse time correlation ($\tau$) scaling of $\log (1/\epsilon)$, where $\epsilon$ represents the bond dimension precision. Furthermore, we establish that VPE-TEBD requires a bond dimension of $\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{polylog}(t/\epsilon))$, dependent on time $t$ and precision $\epsilon$, whereas LPP requires $\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{polylog}(\beta/\epsilon))$, dependent on inverse temperature $\beta$ and precision $\epsilon$. These logarithmic dependencies indicate that both algorithms are capable of simulating long-time dynamics and high-temperature states, respectively, using computationally efficient resources.

This paper introduces a new method for decoupling random variables using what it calls a scale-based approximation of restricted efficacy. This approach generalizes the concept of "restricted efficacy" (or "bounded influence"), which was originally developed to analyze decentralized networks. The summary first outlines the definition of variables that are "k-influenced" and presents the core decoupling theorem applicable to this class. It then defines the scale-based approximation of restricted efficacy and establishes a decoupling result tailored to these variables. Finally, the paper applies these findings to improve the analysis of the "secret sharing" problem within decentralized storage networks.

The color dipole formulation of the proton's parton distribution function (PDF) involves a perturbative series in powers of the strong coupling constant $\alpha_s$ that exhibits infrared renormalons at both $z=-2$ and $z=-4$. We contend that these infrared renormalons are physically significant and must be addressed through the application of principal value prescriptions. Furthermore, we argue that the well-known logarithmic enhancement of the leading logarithmic (LL) BFKL exchange at $z=-2$ is misleading; consequently, the standard LL BFKL result should be revised to incorporate this essential feature.

Transferring the magnetooptical effect into the visible spectrum through strong circular dichroism within photonic structures constitutes a significant area of research. In this work, we present a theoretical investigation of circular dichroism utilizing magnetooptical materials positioned within magnetophonic crystal architectures. Our findings reveal that a circularly polarized incident beam interacting with an all-optical metamaterial lattice exhibits a reflection intensity that varies based on the scanning direction. Specifically, we demonstrate that the structural symmetry dictates the dependence of circular dichroism on scanning direction. By designing structures with C2 symmetry, we achieved a reflection intensity difference of up to 100% between opposite scanning directions for specific combinations of circular polarization and scan path. We attribute this phenomenon to the formation of non-reciprocal Dirac cones within the photonic band structure. Consequently, scanning-direction-dependent circular dichroism emerges as a distinctive optical property of magnetophonic crystals featuring Dirac points.

Decision-based white-box testing involves injecting knowledge into a model to facilitate improvements or enable new applications. In many practical scenarios, however, models operate as opaque black boxes where such knowledge transfer is restricted. This study introduces a method for transferring knowledge from decision-based, information-limited white-box systems to a zero-shot capable neural network. The proposed approach builds upon an existing information-injected technique adapted for conversion to a black-box framework. We validate the method's efficacy through experiments on image classification and object detection tasks, demonstrating a significant enhancement in performance on both natural and synthetic datasets compared to standard baselines.

The dataset comprises $3.0\text{ fb}^{-1}$ of $pp$ collision data. The measured integrated yield for this specific decay channel is $1511\pm130\text{ (stat)}\pm100\text{ (syst)}$ events. Constructing the submodule lattice $\mathcal{L}(M)$ for an arbitrary module $M$ is a nontrivial task. This paper introduces a method to build $\mathcal{L}(M)$ when $M$ is multiplicity-free, utilizing data derived from a selection of submodules. The approach relies on the concept of a "test set" $T \subseteq M$, defined such that for any submodules $X$ and $Y$, the inclusion $X \subseteq Y$ holds if and only if $\dim(T \cap X) \leq \dim(T \cap Y)$. The paper establishes sufficient conditions for a set to qualify as test data and demonstrates how these sets can be practically generated. Additionally, it examines the relationship between this framework and the use of composition factors to characterize module structures.

Imitation learning is a well-established paradigm in artificial intelligence where an agent acquires a task by analyzing expert demonstrations. However, collecting these demonstrations often requires substantial human effort and time. Furthermore, purely imitating experts limits an agent's ability to adapt or surpass current capabilities. To address these issues, this paper introduces a new framework called Co-Imitation Training (Co-IT). In this model, both the agent and a collaborator jointly learn a task, allowing the agent to utilize demonstrations provided by the co-learner rather than relying solely on human input. This approach enables agents to learn more efficiently and effectively, leveraging the agent's own experiences to improve performance. We evaluate Co-IT across three distinct environments: a standard video game, Minecraft, and a robotic arm setup. Our findings indicate that Co-IT significantly accelerates learning speeds and yields superior performance compared to traditional methods.

This study introduces a novel approach to determine the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence within the context of universal source coding. The suggested estimator, which relies on the symmetric form of the KL divergence, demonstrates superior performance across both i.i.d. and non-i.i.d. scenarios when contrasted with existing methods. Furthermore, we establish a fresh theoretical upper bound for the regret associated with this estimator. Leveraging these advancements, we develop an optimized version of the Ziv-Lenk (KL) code, referred to as the Symmetric-Optimal (SO) code. Empirical results indicate that the SO code outperforms the standard Ziv-Lenk (KL) code and the Context-Weighted (CW) code, particularly when dealing with small sample sizes.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) typically generates output by selecting tokens step-by-step using a scoring model, where an associated probability guides a softmax distribution over possible next tokens. Although this approach is straightforward, it often underperforms compared to methods that utilize extensive search algorithms. Conversely, powerful search techniques, while effective, are computationally expensive and impractical for real-time applications. This paper introduces a reinforcement learning framework designed to enhance translation quality by leveraging search-derived training data. We evaluate our approach on both WMT news translation tasks and low-resource scenarios for Catalan, demonstrating that our method outperforms strong baseline systems. Additionally, we provide an in-depth analysis of the learned policy, the search trajectories, and the specific challenges inherent to the NMT task.

We present the analysis of experimental and theoretical non-equilibrium steady states achieved by periodically driving a superconducting qubit coupled to a harmonic oscillator. Our work includes a detailed theoretical modeling of the system's behavior and an experimental assessment of the qubit's properties under various driving protocols. Specifically, we investigate the quality factors, transition frequencies, and initial quantum states, while analyzing how these elements influence the system's dynamics. Our results demonstrate that a non-equilibrium steady state can be established within this driven architecture. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive theoretical framework that accurately accounts for the observed experimental phenomena.

This paper investigates the theory of recurrent structures within biharmonic hypersurfaces located in Euclidean space. We establish that if the structure adheres to three specific mechanisms—parallelism, recurrent behavior, or pseudo-recurrence—it cannot exist, as these conditions lead to a contradiction. Consequently, no biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ ($n\geq 3$) can possess these recurrent or related geometric properties.

A subset $S$ of the positive integers $\mathbb{Z}_+$ is termed $(p/q)$-identifiable if, for any two infinite sequences of elements drawn from $S$, the sequence formed by concatenating them in order with $p$ copies of the first and $q$ copies of the second can be uniquely decomposed back into its original components. This paper investigates the structural properties of $(p/q)$-identifiable sets and establishes that every such set must possess a specific form. Furthermore, we introduce a practical algorithm to determine whether an arbitrary subset of $\mathbb{Z}_+$ qualifies as $(p/q)$-identifiable.

MongoDB is a prevalent NoSQL database that supports multi-document transactions, yet it lacks formal guarantees regarding transactional coherence. This deficiency allows applications to experience interleaved commits, where a transaction completes before another, but the finishing transaction of the second occurs prior to the first's completion. Such non-serializable behaviors can compromise data integrity. To address this, we introduce a lightweight, practical coherence checker specifically designed for MongoDB. Our methodology involves reverse-engineering the instance's commit order from the commit logs stored in the opjournal. Our findings, based on a real-world deployment of MongoDB 4.2, reveal that interleaved commits occur with high frequency. Furthermore, we observed that interleaving patterns vary significantly across different workloads and versions of the database.
